description: En Raptor Squad creemos en el poder de la sinergia y la tecnología para resolver problemas del mundo real. Somos una manada multidisciplinaria de desarrolladores, creativos y estrategas unidos por una misma misión: diseñar, codear y entregar una solución innovadora antes de que el cronómetro llegue a cero
summary: Lunaria is a web-based astronaut simulator for children aged 7 to 12. Players take on the role of Alex Ríos and, accompanied by a robot named Titus, embark on an expedition that spans from the launchpad to an outpost on the Moon. In each level, players must prepare life support, energy, and propulsion systems; align the spacecraft; manage resources; execute a landing; and analyze a sample of regolith. Titus explains the mission objectives and presents information cards containing real-world data linked to NASA. The spacecraft’s resources and operational tolerances serve as key parameters within the simulator.
details:
Lunaria is a web-based simulator of a fictional lunar expedition, designed for children aged 7 to 12. Players control Alex Ríos as they navigate the spacecraft and the lunar surface. Titus, a robotic guide, points out the next objective and provides access to information cards containing real-world data, complete with links to NASA.

The game begins at a terminal menu. If no saved expedition exists, a cinematic sequence displays the launchpad. The experience is divided into six stages: preparing air, energy, and propulsion while still on Earth; navigating the spacecraft, aligning its course, and recording a fictional radio signal; repairing an electrical fault and managing power distribution; selecting a landing site; setting up a habitat and analyzing regolith; and maintaining the outpost for three cycles. Each stage features a unique console interface. Progress is saved within the browser, allowing players to resume their campaign or select any previously unlocked mission.

Exploration is rendered using a 2D Canvas, featuring a top-down view of the spacecraft, collision detection, and eight-directional sprites for Alex and Titus. Three.js is utilized exclusively for the two cinematic sequences in the first level—housed in a separate file—to ensure that navigating the spacecraft remains lightweight and responsive. Music and sound effects are generated directly within the browser; notably, the engine sounds cease once the craft reaches space. The game defaults to English, with an option in the main menu to switch to Spanish. Settings for volume, animations, and language are stored locally on the user's device.

Children can play without the need for any installations, using a keyboard, mouse, or touch controls. Through the decision-making process, players learn about life support systems, signal latency, lunar gravity, and regolith—with the ability to view the original sources for the information provided. Features such as large buttons, clear visual focus, a low-animation mode, and bilingual support ensure the game is accessible to a wide range of users.

The intended impact is for the game to serve as an engaging, playable space mission—whether at home or in the classroom—designed to spark curiosity about the Moon and help children learn to distinguish between factual, source-based data and the rules established specifically for the game. The beta version now covers the entire journey, from the launch site to the lunar outpost.

The code is written in JavaScript, using React 19 and Vite, with an interface styled in CSS. The models—the spacecraft, Alex, and Titus—are built using Three.js, exported as GLB files for refinement in Blender, and then converted into PNG images via a script that utilizes Microsoft Edge. Automated testing is handled by Node.js and Playwright, running within the Edge browser. Players simply need a modern web browser on a computer or tablet.

Creativity shines through both the artwork and the gameplay mechanics. The models are original; the deck is designed with a sense of volume, yet navigated like a 2D floor plan. The console interface shifts with each level. Subtitles replace recorded dialogue, and sound effects are synthesized in real-time. The silence of the engines while in orbit is an intentional part of the narrative.

The development team prioritized several key aspects: tailoring the experience to the target age group, establishing clear objectives, and ensuring that every player decision has a logical basis. Scientific integrity was also a focus—references to NASA are included, and the spacecraft’s resources are presented as functional game mechanics. Furthermore, the team optimized performance by limiting 3D elements to cinematic sequences, ensured accessibility through keyboard, touch, and reduced-motion support, and guaranteed that the gameplay experience remains consistent across both English and Spanish versions.
